title_en: On the Resurrection of the Dead
author: Athenagoras
occasion: Athenagoras writes to defend the Christian doctrine of bodily resurrection against those who disbelieve or doubt it, and to show that resurrection is both possible for God and consistent with God's purpose, human nature, and divine justice.
argument: Athenagoras first argues that disbelief in resurrection is unreasonable unless critics can prove it is impossible or unwilled by God. He shows that God's knowledge and power make resurrection possible, and that apparent difficulties such as bodies eaten by animals do not prevent it because only what is truly proper food can be united to a body. He then argues from God's purpose in creating humans, from human nature as a compound of soul and body, and from divine justice, which requires that the whole human being receive reward or punishment. Finally, he argues from the proper end of human life, which belongs to the complete human being, not to the soul alone.

outline.move: Introduces the need to defend the truth about resurrection and sets the standard that critics must show resurrection to be impossible or unwilled by God.
Argues that resurrection is possible for God, answering objections about bodies destroyed or eaten by animals through a detailed account of digestion and what can truly become part of a body.
Shows that resurrection is not unwilled by God, because it is neither unjust nor unworthy of God.
Provides a methodological aside distinguishing arguments about the truth from arguments for the truth, and explains when each is more useful.
Argues from God's purpose in creating humans that the whole human being must endure, which requires resurrection.
Discusses the proper ordering of arguments, noting that many wrongly make judgment the sole cause of resurrection.
Argues from human nature as a compound of immortal soul and body that the whole human being must endure, which requires resurrection.
Argues from divine justice that the whole human being, not the soul alone, must receive reward or punishment, and that this requires the resurrection of the body.
Argues from the proper end of human life, which belongs to the complete human being of soul and body, so that resurrection is necessary for that end to be reached.

cast.name: Athenagoras
cast.who: The author, a Christian philosopher defending the resurrection.

cast.name: God
cast.who: The creator and judge whose power, wisdom, and justice ground the argument.

cast.name: Critics
cast.who: Those who disbelieve or doubt the resurrection, including some who raise objections about bodies eaten by animals.

cast.name: Thyestes
cast.who: Mythological figure cited by critics as an example of cannibalism.

voices.speaker: Critics (objectors)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by phrases such as 'which especially seemed to trouble some' (ὃ δὴ καὶ μάλιστα ταράττειν ἔδοξέ τινας) and 'These people say' (Οὗτοι δέ γέ φασιν).

voices.speaker: The apostle (unnamed in the text, traditionally identified as Paul)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'according to the apostle' (κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον).

key_terms.sense: The resurrection of dead human bodies to form the same human beings again.
The compound of soul and body that constitutes the complete human being.
The immortal rational soul, which alone is not the complete human being.
The body, which together with the soul makes up the human being and must be raised.
Food that is truly assimilated to a body; only what is proper and natural food can become part of a body.
The nature of a thing, especially human nature as a compound of soul and body.
God's just judgment of human deeds, requiring the whole human being to be present.
God's providential care over creation, including just oversight of human actions.
The proper end or goal of human life, belonging to the complete human being.
Continuance or lasting existence, especially the enduring existence of the whole human being.
Incorruptibility, the state of the risen body no longer subject to decay.
Justice, especially God's justice in rewarding or punishing the whole human being.
The purpose or intention of God in creating human beings.

scripture: The author cites the apostle Paul's statement that the corruptible must put on incorruption, and alludes to the commandments such as 'Honor your father and mother' and 'You shall not commit adultery.' These commandments are presented as examples of laws given to humans, not souls alone, as part of the argument that judgment must apply to the whole human being. Biblical books are not cited by name in the surviving text.
uncertain: The exact identity of the original addressee or audience beyond those interested in the resurrection.
Whether the work originally contained more explicit scriptural citations now lost.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The apostle (unnamed in the text, traditionally identified as Paul)... Introduced by 'according to the apostle' (κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον).
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text does not contain the phrase 'according to the apostle' (κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον) or any reference to an apostle. The brief appears to be importing a detail from a different text or edition. Section 18 refers to 'the corruptible must put on incorruption' without naming Paul or using the phrase 'according to the apostle.'

The Median table: 'that Median table' — the source has τὴν Μηδικὴν τράπεζαν ἐκείνην ('that Median table'), with the demonstrative ἐκείνην ('that') indicating a specific, notorious historical/mythological reference. The brief's rendering omits this demonstrative force.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He shows that God's knowledge and power make resurrection possible, and that apparent difficulties such as bodies eaten by animals do not prevent it because only what is truly proper food can be united to a body.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀποχωροῦντα δὲ τῆς θρεπτικῆς δυνάμεως, καὶ σκιδνάμενα πρὸς ἐκεῖνα πάλιν ἐξ ὧν τὴν πρώτην ἔσχε σύστασιν, ἑνοῦται μὲν τούτοις ἐφ᾿ ὅσον ἂν ἕκαστον τύχῃ χρόνον· ἐκεῖθεν δὲ διακριθέντα πάλιν σοφίᾳ καὶ δυνάμει τοῦ πᾶσαν ζώου φύσιν σὺν ταῖς οἰκείαις δυνάμεσι συγκρίναντος ἑνοῦται προσφυῶς ἕκαστον ἑκάστῳ
_unresolved_facts.fix: He shows that God's knowledge and power make resurrection possible, and that apparent difficulties such as bodies eaten by animals do not prevent it because what is consumed either passes through as non-nutritive or, even if temporarily absorbed, is not permanently part of the body but returns to the elements, from which God can reassemble each part to its proper place by his wisdom and power.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['9', '10']: 'Shows that resurrection is not unwilled by God, because it is neither unjust nor unworthy of God.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀλλὰ μὴν οὐδ᾿ ἀβούλητον. Τὸ γὰρ ἀβούλητον ἢ ὡς ἄδικον αὐτῷ ἐστιν ἀβούλητον ἢ ὡς ἀνάξιον.
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections ['9', '10']: 'Shows that resurrection is not unwilled by God, because it is neither unjust (to any other being or to the one raised) nor unworthy of God.' — Section 10 explicitly adds that it cannot be unjust to the one raised (οὐδ᾿ ἐκεῖνο φῆσαι δυνατὸν ὡς περὶ αὐτὸν θεωρεῖταί τις ἀδικία τὸν ἀνιστάμενον ἄνθρωπον), which the brief omits.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['11']: 'Provides a methodological aside distinguishing arguments about the truth from arguments for the truth, and explains when each is more useful.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ ὅτι μὲν ἕτερος ὁ περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας λόγος, ἕτερος δὲ ὁ ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας, εἴρηται διὰ τῶν προλαβόντων μετρίως... Ἰτέον δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον, καὶ δεικτέον ἀληθῆ τὸν περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως λόγον ἀπό τε τῆς αἰτίας αὐτῆς
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections ['11']: 'Recapitulates the distinction between arguments about the truth and arguments for the truth, then transitions to demonstrating the truth of the resurrection from its cause (God's purpose in creation), human nature, and divine judgment.' — The section is not merely methodological but actively transitions to the positive demonstration, beginning with the argument from cause.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ['14']: 'Discusses the proper ordering of arguments, noting that many wrongly make judgment the sole cause of resurrection.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πολλοὶ γὰρ τὸν τῆς ἀναστάσεως λόγον διαλαμβάνοντες τῷ τρίτῳ μόνῳ τὴν πᾶσαν ἐπήρεισαν αἰτίαν, νομίσαντες τὴν αἰτίαν γίνεσθαι διὰ τὴν κρίσιν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: sections ['14']: 'Discusses the proper ordering of arguments and explicitly states that many wrongly rest the entire cause of resurrection on the third argument alone (judgment), having thought that the cause comes about through judgment; but since all rise yet not all are judged, this is shown false, and resurrection is primarily due to God's creative purpose and human nature.' — The brief's 'sole cause' understates the explicit critique that judgment cannot be the cause since infants who have done nothing rise too.
